opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a great question, and one I think about a lot. Right now clinical trials carry an enormous burden. They're really the first place where we learn, at scale, whether a molecule does what we hoped in a human body and whether it does something we *didn't* hope for. So much of the attrition we see, the roughly ninety percent of drugs that fail once they enter the clinic, comes from discovering toxicity or a lack of efficacy that we just couldn't see earlier.

As predictive models get better, I think the role of the trial starts to shift. Today it's a discovery process; you learn things in it. In the future it becomes much more of a confirmation process. If you can model, with real confidence, how a molecule binds not just to its intended target but to the thousands of other proteins in the body, and how that plays out in terms of off-target effects and toxicity, then by the time something reaches a patient you've already filtered out a huge fraction of the failure modes. The trial is then confirming a hypothesis you're fairly sure of, rather than searching in the dark.

That has a few knock-on effects. First, I'd hope trials become smaller and faster, because you're designing molecules that are much more likely to succeed and you can target the right patient populations from the start. Second, there's the idea of designing trials around the model's predictions: using computational understanding to stratify patients, choose dosing, and pick endpoints far more intelligently. And over time, as these models are validated against real clinical outcomes, I think regulators will become more comfortable with in silico evidence as part of the package. That isn't replacing human trials, but it changes what we need to prove in them.

But I want to be careful here. We're not at the point where a model replaces the trial, and patient safety has to remain paramount. The way you earn that trust is the way you earn it in any science: you make predictions, you test them against reality, and you build up a track record. The feedback loop matters too. Every trial generates data that should flow back into the models and make them better. So I see it as a virtuous cycle rather than a replacement, where the computation and the clinic get more and more tightly coupled, and the whole system gets dramatically more efficient at getting the right medicines to the right patients.

r001.rationale: The response says that as predictive models improve, trials will shift from discovery toward confirmation, with trials designed around model predictions and becoming smaller and faster.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something I think about a lot, because the clinical trial is really where the whole system bottlenecks right now. If you look at the end-to-end process of getting a drug to a patient, the computational side has gotten dramatically faster and cheaper, but the trial is still this ten-year, billion-dollar thing that looks structurally almost identical to how it looked decades ago. And the reason it looks like that is that it was designed for a world where we had essentially no predictive power. You run the experiment on humans because you have no other way to find out what happens.

So the first thing I'd say is that as the models get better, I think the trial starts to look less like an experiment and more like a verification step. Right now a huge fraction of what a trial is doing is discovery. You're discovering the toxicity profile, you're discovering which subpopulations respond, you're discovering the off-target effects. If you have a model that's genuinely good at predicting drug-drug interactions and toxicity, a lot of that discovery moves earlier, into the computational phase, and the trial becomes about confirming a prediction rather than generating one from scratch. That's a very different shape of experiment. You can design it to be smaller and more targeted, because you're testing a specific hypothesis the model has produced rather than casting a wide net.

The second thing, and I think this is the more interesting one, is that the trial itself becomes a source of training data in a much tighter loop. Today the information coming out of trials is quite lossy. A lot of it ends up in a PDF, the negative results often don't get reported at all, and the structure of the data isn't really designed to feed back into a model. If you think of the whole thing as a learning system, that's a huge waste. The failed trial is arguably the most valuable data point you have, because it's exactly where the model was wrong. So I'd want trials to be designed with the explicit goal of maximising the information they give back to the predictive models. That means collecting richer phenotypic data, being systematic about the negatives, and instrumenting the trial so that the gap between what you predicted and what you observed is something you can actually measure and learn from.

And then there's a regulatory question which I think people underestimate. Regulators are, quite rightly, conservative. They're not going to accept a model's prediction in place of human safety data anytime soon, and I don't think they should. But what I think can happen is that model predictions start to shape where you look. If the model says this compound is very likely to have a hepatotoxicity issue in a particular genotype, you can enrich for that in your trial design, you can monitor for it more closely, and you can stop earlier if it shows up. So the model doesn't replace the trial, it makes the trial a much sharper instrument.

The thing I'd push back on is the idea that the endpoint is a world with no trials at all. I don't think that's right, at least not for a long time. Biology is extremely good at surprising you. What I think happens instead is that the trial gets progressively compressed from the ends inward. The early-phase stuff, the dose-finding, the toxicity screening, that gets eaten by prediction first. The late-phase efficacy work is the last to go, because that's where the models have the least ground truth and the stakes are highest. And honestly, the thing that would accelerate all of this most is just getting the data out of its silos, because the models are only as good as what they've seen, and right now they've seen a tiny fraction of what's actually been measured.

r001.rationale: The response says better predictions should shift trials from broad discovery toward smaller, targeted verification studies, with models guiding what to monitor and when to stop.

astra-6.text:
I think the opportunity is to make clinical trials much more informed by what we can predict before we get into humans. Can we identify which patients are most likely to benefit, which combinations are worth testing, and where we should be particularly careful about toxicity? That could help us design trials that give us clearer answers and expose fewer patients to treatments that aren’t going to work for them.

But you have to distinguish a prediction from evidence. A model might perform very well on the data we already have and still miss something important in a new patient population. So I’d want to see these predictions tested prospectively, with uncertainty made explicit, before they start driving consequential trial decisions.

Ultimately, I think there’s a really interesting feedback loop: models help us design better experiments, and those experiments generate the data that makes the models better. Clinical trials remain essential, but we can become much more deliberate about what we’re trying to learn from each one.

r001.rationale: The response proposes making trials more informed by predictions made before human testing, using them to choose patients and combinations and improve trial design. This communicates evolving trial approaches to benefit from predictive models.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the opportunity is to make clinical trials much more informed by what we can predict before a drug ever reaches a patient. If we can get better at predicting toxicity and interactions, we can make better decisions about which molecules to take forward, which patients might benefit, and what we need to monitor.

But the crucial distinction is between a prediction and evidence. You still need to establish safety and efficacy in humans. So I’d expect an evolution where models help us design more targeted trials, and those trials generate the data that allows us to test and improve the models.

And uncertainty matters enormously here. It’s not enough for a model to give you an answer; you need to understand where that answer is reliable and where you’re operating beyond what the model has seen. The exciting possibility is that we learn more from every patient enrolled, while exposing fewer people to treatments that are unlikely to help.

r001.rationale: The response says improved predictions of toxicity and interactions should inform decisions and help design more targeted clinical trials.
